title: What Is in the Box: A Release Bundle With a Manifest That Checks Itself, and the Four Ways Files Differ From It

questions.question: A download stops half way. What in the manifest finds it?
options: The end line, which holds the hash of everything above it: its absence is no end line, and a changed manifest is bad checksum
questions.explanation: The most common damage there is.

questions.question: Why is the manifest sorted by path?
options: The same release in any order gives the same text, so the manifest can itself be compared and hashed

questions.question: Why does the manifest refuse ../../etc/passwd as a path?
options: The updater writes at that path: an archive that escapes the directory overwrites the system unpacking it, and the manifest has to refuse it before any file is written
questions.explanation: Only 4 of 15 test paths were accepted.

questions.question: Which difference can a size check not see?
options: A byte changed in place: same size, different hash

questions.question: Why is a stale file from an older release a problem?
options: It is part of what is running, since a program may load it by name, and it is not part of the release

questions.question: Why is FNV-1a not enough for a real release?
options: Anyone can recompute it: a real release is signed with a key kept at the build machine, which needs a cryptographic library this curriculum does not write
